archaeology.description: Registered evidence includes the Tel Dan and Ein Gev inscriptions, Hazael-named artifacts from Arslan Tash, Samos, and Nimrud, and the Melqart Stele near Aleppo; these finds document connections and activity associated with Aram-Damascus without defining its full territory.
archaeology.short_description: Inscriptions and artifacts linked to Hazael and Aram-Damascus document regional connections without defining the polity's full territory.

geography.description: Centered on Damascus in modern Syria, Aram-Damascus is associated with the Barada River and a southern-Levantine setting; the mapped point is an approximate reference.
geography.short_description: Aram-Damascus centered on Damascus and the Barada River in southern Syria and the southern Levant.

Hamath.name: Hamath
Hamath.fall: 720 BC (conquered by Sargon II of Assyria)

archaeology.description: Registered evidence includes the Zakkur Stele at Tell Afis, Hamath inscriptions, and Hama graffiti; these inscriptional records document rulers, languages, and everyday writing associated with Hamath.
archaeology.short_description: The Zakkur Stele, Hamath inscriptions, and Hama graffiti provide substantial written evidence for the polity.

geography.description: Hamath was centered at Hama on the Orontes River in central Syria; its mapped location is a regional reference near Luash, Bit-Agusi, and Aram-Damascus.
geography.short_description: Hamath centered on Hama along the Orontes River in central Syria.

archaeology.description: Registered evidence includes the Arslan Tash Ivory Inscription, found at the former Bit-Adini capital after the Assyrian conquest; the dataset also lists other nearby finds without assigning them to this polity.

geography.description: Bit-Adini occupied territory on both banks of the Euphrates below Carchemish, centered at Til Barsip (Tell Ahmar); its mapped point is a regional reference.
geography.short_description: Bit-Adini occupied both banks of the Euphrates below Carchemish, centered at Til Barsip.

Bit-Gabbar.name: Bit-Gabbar

archaeology.description: Registered evidence from Zincirli includes royal inscriptions, funerary stelae, the Kilamuwa Scepter, and monumental sculptures such as the citadel gate lions and Bar-Rakib relief; together these records document Sam'al's political, mortuary, and artistic life.
archaeology.short_description: Zincirli's inscriptions, funerary stelae, artifacts, and sculptures document Sam'al's political and artistic life.

geography.description: Bit-Gabbar was centered on Sam'al at Zincirli in southeastern Anatolia, near the Karasu River; its mapped point is a regional reference among northern Syrian and Anatolian polities.
geography.short_description: Bit-Gabbar centered on Sam'al at Zincirli near the Karasu River in southeastern Anatolia.

Pattin-Unqi.name: ʿUmqā
Pattin-Unqi.etymology: The name ʿUmqā is associated with the Aramaic root ʿ-m-q, meaning ‘deep’ or ‘depth’. It may refer to the low-lying Amuq plain or its geographical setting. This interpretation does not by itself establish the polity’s ethnic identity or prove how every ancient source named the region.

archaeology.short_description: No polity-specific archaeological evidence is currently registered for Pattin-Unqi.

geography.short_description: Pattin-Unqi centered on Kunulua in the Amuq Plain along the Orontes corridor of southeastern Turkey.
